appraisal_events.evidence: "le plus dangereux de tous les recels, c'est celui de la faute elle-même dans l'esprit du coupable"; Charlus's habitual defensive speeches 'ôtait leurs derniers doutes...inspirait leurs premiers'; at the staircase, after Basin's slip about his 'goûts spéciaux', Charlus himself insists on returning to the phrase like 'les coupables qui...croient devoir prolonger une conversation périlleuse'.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator directly asserts that Charlus's protective denials and defensive rhetoric repeatedly betray the very secret they mean to hide, a pattern reenacted when he presses Basin to repeat the remark about his 'special tastes' rather than letting it drop.

appraisal_events.evidence: "dévorée des yeux par des femmes, des hommes, qui cherchaient à surprendre le secret de son élégance et de sa beauté"; Mme de Gallardon, unable to secure a greeting, 'tournait le dos pour ne pas avoir l'air de la voir' and vents spiteful gossip about her aging; the prince de Sagan pays her an elaborate, almost historical homage with his hat.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator frames the duchesse as the visible center of admiration and ceremonious homage among the departing guests, a status underscored by contrast with Gallardon's failed snub and envious gossip.

status_effects.explanation: His attempts at self-protective speech are shown by the narrator to be self-incriminating, lowering how trustworthy his own account of himself appears.
By anxiously prolonging the dangerous exchange about his 'goûts spéciaux' instead of letting Basin's slip pass, Charlus loses control of the exchange he means to master.

The narrator explicitly parallels her vague, overinsistent praise of Charlus with his own self-betraying denials, so her secret passion is likewise exposed by the words meant to mask it, culminating in her blush and surrendered letter.
She is the visible center of admiration and elaborate ceremonious homage (Sagan's bow) among the departing guests.
Her failure to secure Oriane's greeting, and her spiteful gossip framed by the narrator as motivated by jealousy, comparatively diminish her standing next to the admired duchesse.

ambiguities: The princesse de Guermantes's status effect rests on the narrator's explicit structural parallel with Charlus's self-betraying rhetoric ('de la même façon que faisait parfois M. de Charlus lui-même') rather than on a directly quoted evaluative act, making her exposure somewhat inferential.

Mme de Gallardon's disparaging remarks about Oriane ('elle commence à vieillir...méchante comme une teigne') are reported as speech clearly motivated by jealousy and are not endorsed by the narrator as accurate; they are read here as evidence of Gallardon's own diminishment rather than as a credible blame of the duchesse.
